summary: Provides a framework and requirements for operations, administration and maintenance (OAM) of Layer 2 VPN services, pseudowires and packet switched network tunnels. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a customer reports that their Layer 2 VPN is down, the provider needs to work out where the break is: in the customer's line, in the provider's own network, or in the carrier underneath. This memo sets out how maintenance checks should be layered so that each part of the network looks after its own, and what each check has to be able to do.

questions: what is a maintenance end point
subtitle: How to maintain, monitor and troubleshoot Layer 2 virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: A provider that sells Layer 2 VPN services has to be able to tell when a service is broken, where it is broken and how bad it is, without the customer's own equipment cooperating.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines an OAM framework in which every layer of the service has its own maintenance entities, and then lists requirements for VPLS and VPWS: discovery, fault detection, verification and localization, alarm suppression, and loss, delay and jitter measurement.
tldr.outcome: The framework borrows the concepts of IEEE 802.1ag and ITU-T Y.1731 and extends them to the L2VPN service layer, so that the same fault is reported once at the level it happened.

today: RFC 6136 is an Informational document from March 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is a framework and a list of requirements rather than a protocol, so the mechanisms it describes were still to be worked out elsewhere.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
The scope of OAM for any service or transport infrastructure technology can be very broad. OSI has defined five generic functional areas, commonly abbreviated as FCAPS: Fault Management, Configuration Management, Accounting Management, Performance Management and Security Management. This document focuses on the Fault and Performance Management aspects; the others are for further study.

Fault Management can be viewed in terms of several categories. Fault detection deals with mechanisms that can detect hard failures, such as link and device failures, and soft failures, such as software failure, memory corruption and misconfiguration. Typically a lightweight protocol is desirable to detect the fault, and it is prudent to verify the fault before taking further steps to isolate it. Once a fault along the data path has been verified, it is important to be able to isolate it to the level of a given device or link. A fault notification mechanism can work with a detection mechanism to notify the devices upstream and downstream of the detection point, including sending a forward fault notification from the server layer to the client layer networks in the format appropriate to that layer, and backward notifications where applicable. Fault recovery deals with recovering from the detected failure by switching to an alternate available data path, using alternate devices or links.

Performance Management deals with mechanisms that allow determining and measuring the performance of the network or services under consideration. It can be used to verify compliance with both service-level and network-level metric objectives. It typically consists of measurement of performance metrics such as frame loss, frame delay and frame delay variation, also called jitter, across managed entities when those entities are in an available state; performance management is suspended across unavailable managed entities.

The document provides a reference model for OAM as it relates to L2VPN services and their associated pseudowires and packet switched network tunnels. OAM requirements for the L2VPN services are identified, and where those requirements impose requirements on pseudowire or packet switched network OAM, those are identified too.
sections.plainLanguage: The work splits into two families of checks. Fault checks find a break, confirm it is real, work out which device or link it is at, tell the neighbours, and switch traffic to a spare path. Performance checks measure loss, delay and jitter. The memo covers only these two families; configuration, accounting and security management are left for later.

sections.title: The OAM Framework: Domains, End Points and Intermediate Points
sections.content:
The point-to-point or bridged LAN functionality of an L2VPN is emulated by a network of Provider Edges to which the Customer Edges are connected. That network can belong to a single network operator or span several, and to a single service provider or span several. Each layer is responsible for its own OAM.

An OAM domain is a network region over which OAM frames operate unobstructed. At the edge of a domain, filtering constructs should prevent OAM frames from exiting and entering that domain. OAM domains can be nested but not overlapped: in a hierarchy, the OAM frames of a higher-level domain pass transparently through the lower-level domains, while the OAM frames of a lower-level domain are blocked or filtered at the edge of that domain. Each domain can be associated with the level at which it operates; higher-level domains can contain lower-level ones, but not the other way round, and a higher-level domain does not necessarily mean a higher numerical value in the level encoding. A PE can be part of several OAM domains, with each interface belonging to the same or a different domain. A PE with an interface at the boundary of an OAM domain must block outgoing OAM frames, filter out incoming frames whose domain level is lower than or the same as the one configured on that interface, and pass through frames whose domain level is higher.

Generically, L2VPNs consist of a customer OAM domain, a service provider OAM domain and network operator OAM domains. The domains can be categorized as hierarchical, resulting from OAM layering and implying a contractual agreement among the owning entities, or adjacent, typically independent of each other with no relationship among them.

Maintenance End Points are responsible for origination and termination of OAM frames and are located at the edge of their OAM domains. Maintenance Intermediate Points are located within their domains; they normally pass OAM frames but never initiate them. An OAM frame is generally associated with a Maintenance Entity Group, which consists of a set of Maintenance Entities associated with the same service instance. A Maintenance Entity is a point-to-point association between a pair of MEPs and represents a monitored entity. For example, in a VPLS involving n customer edges, all the entities associated with the VPLS in the customer OAM domain can be considered part of a VPLS MEG, where the n-point MEG consists of a maximum of n(n-1)/2 entities. MEPs and MIPs correspond to a PE, or more specifically to an interface of a PE, and a MEP on a PE receives messages from the other MEPs of the group, some of which may reside on the same PE. In hierarchical domains, a MEP of a lower-level domain can correspond to a MIP or a MEP of a higher-level domain, and the MIPs of a lower-level domain are always transparent to the higher-level domain. OAM at each layer should be independent of other layers, so MEPs and MIPs at each layer are identified with layer-specific identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of the network is its own maintenance area, and the areas can sit inside one another. A check started by a customer stays inside the customer's area, while a check started by the provider passes through it untouched, because the provider's check is the higher level. At the edge of each area sit the end points that start and stop checks, and between them sit intermediate points that only pass checks along.

sections.title: The VPLS Framework
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service is used in several contexts, and the document separates them: a bridged LAN service over networks, some of which are MPLS or IP; an MPLS or IP network supporting those bridged LAN services; and LAN emulation.

The most common definition is a bridged LAN service over an MPLS or IP network. The service coverage is end-to-end from user network interface to user network interface among the customer edge devices, and it provides a virtual LAN service to the attached customer edges belonging to that service instance. It is called a bridged LAN service because the provider edge performing this end-to-end virtual LAN service is performing bridging functions, either full or a subset, and the definition includes both the bridge module and the LAN emulation module. A VPLS instance is analogous to a VLAN in IEEE 802.1Q networks, and where part of the provider network is Ethernet based, such as with QinQ access, there is a one-to-one correspondence between a VPLS instance and its corresponding provider VLAN. To check the end-to-end service integrity, the OAM mechanism has to cover the end-to-end VPLS from attachment circuit to attachment circuit, including the bridge module, the VPLS forwarder and the associated pseudowires.

The same word is also used for the underlying network that supports bridged LAN services, which can be an end-to-end MPLS or IP network or a hybrid of an MPLS or IP core with an Ethernet access network, made up of VPLS-capable provider edges arranged in a hierarchical, distributed, multi-tier or star topology. Checking the integrity of that network regardless of its topology needs network-level OAM mechanisms such as OAM for MPLS or IP networks, and the discussion of network-level OAM is outside the scope of this document.

VPLS is also used to mean LAN emulation, where it refers only to the full mesh of pseudowires with split horizon that emulates a LAN segment over an MPLS or IP network for a given service instance and its associated VPLS forwarder. The OAM mechanisms in this context refer primarily to the integrity check of VPLS forwarders and their associated full mesh of pseudowires, and to the ability to detect and notify a partial mesh failure.

Because the end-to-end service can span many kinds of network, on the access side a bridged network such as IEEE 802.1ad or IEEE 802.1ah, and in the core IP, MPLS, ATM or SONET, the OAM mechanisms have to apply to all of them. Each such network may be associated with a separate administrative domain, and multiple networks may be associated with a single administrative domain. The OAM mechanisms must be independent of the underlying transport mechanisms and rely on VPLS alone, so that the transparency of OAM mechanisms is ensured over MPLS, IP and other transport technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS is used loosely for three different things: the service the customer buys, the provider network that carries it, and the emulation of a LAN segment that sits on top. Each needs different checks. The service needs end-to-end checks across the whole path; the network needs checks that work whatever its shape; and the emulation needs checks that spot a broken link in the mesh of pseudowires.

sections.title: The VPLS OAM Requirements
sections.content:
These requirements apply to VPLS provider edges offering VPLS as an Ethernet bridged LAN service. The performance metrics used in the requirements are based on MEF 10.1 and RFC 2544. OAM solutions that meet the requirements may make use of existing OAM mechanisms such as Ethernet OAM or VCCV, but they must not break those existing mechanisms; if extensions are required, they should be coordinated with the groups responsible for them.

Discovery allows a VPLS-aware device to learn about other devices that support the same VPLS instance within a given domain, and to learn enough information, such as IP and MAC addresses, for OAM frames to be exchanged (R1). Proactive connectivity monitoring is required to ensure the service, so VPLS OAM must allow proactive connectivity monitoring between two VPLS-aware devices supporting the same instance (R2a), fault verification once a fault has been detected (R2b), and fault localization (R2c). A single transport or network fault may cause several services to fail at once and so produce several service alarms, so VPLS OAM must support fault notification triggered as a result of transport or network faults, and that notification should be used to suppress redundant service-level alarms at the client layer (R2d).

Performance measurement requirements follow. A VPLS may be degraded if service frames are lost in transit, so per-service frame loss measurement is required (R3). A VPLS may also be sensitive to delay, and two kinds of measurement are used: one-way delay, which characterizes applications such as multicast and broadcast and usually requires clock synchronization between the two devices, and two-way or round-trip delay, which does not require clock synchronization and is usually sufficient. Two-way delay measurement is required and one-way delay measurement should be supported (R4a, R4b). Frame delay variation is measured with one-way mechanisms, which are considered sufficient (R5).

Availability needs no separate requirement, since it can be tied to connectivity, loss, delay and delay variation measurements. If the OAM frames flow across a different path from the service frames, accurate measurement of the service state may not be possible, so the OAM frames must be forwarded along the same path, that is, the same links and nodes, as the VPLS frames (R6). The mechanism must be scalable enough that a service-aware device can support OAM for each VPLS it supports, even if the OAM is used only for a few premium instances (R7). It must be extensible so that new functions and information elements can be introduced later while keeping backward compatibility, and it must be defined so that devices which do not support OAM can forward the OAM frames in the same fashion as regular VPLS data frames (R8a, R8b).

OAM frames belonging to an OAM domain originate and terminate within that domain, so an OAM domain must be able to filter OAM frames to prevent them leaking outside it, and frames from outside must be discarded when they belong to the same level or a lower-level domain and passed transparently when they belong to a higher-level domain (R9a, R9b, R9c). VPLS OAM must be independent of the underlying transport and network technologies and of their specific OAM capabilities, though it may allow adaptation or interworking with them, for example so that fault notifications from the transport layer can be sent to the VPLS layer (R10a, R10b). It must also be independent of the application technologies and of application OAM: a VPLS may carry IP traffic, but VPLS OAM should not assume IP or rely on IP-level OAM functions (R11a).
sections.plainLanguage: Read the requirements as a checklist for a maintenance system. Find the other devices on the same service, keep checking the link while it is healthy, and when it fails confirm it, locate it and tell the layer above so that one fault does not raise a flood of alarms. Measure loss, delay and jitter, and send the check traffic down the same path as the real traffic.

sections.title: VPWS and Pseudowire Requirements
sections.content:
The VPWS requirements repeat the same structure for the point-to-point service, with numbers from R12 to R23. Discovery lets a VPWS-aware device learn about other devices that support the same VPWS instance within a domain, and enough information to exchange OAM frames (R12). Proactive connectivity monitoring between two VPWS-aware devices is required (R13a), and the mechanism should allow detection of mis-branching or mis-connections (R13b), which is a fault specific to a point-to-point service where a circuit is patched to the wrong place. Fault verification (R13c) and fault localization follow, the latter possibly identifying the specific attachment circuit or pseudowire that is causing the fault. Fault notification triggered by transport or network faults must be supported, and backward fault notification should be supported (R13e, R13f).

Performance measurement requirements follow the same pattern: frame loss (R14), two-way frame delay as a requirement and one-way frame delay as a should (R15a, R15b), and frame delay variation (R16). OAM frames must be forwarded along the same path as the service frames, and for VPWS also using the transfer plane, that is, the data plane (R17a, R17b). Scalability (R18), extensibility and the ability of devices without OAM to forward the frames (R19a, R19b), domain isolation and transparency for higher-level domains (R20a, R20b, R20c), and transport independence (R21a, R21b) are required as they are for VPLS. Application independence is required (R22a), and VPWS OAM should support configurable prioritization of OAM messages (R23).

Where VPLS is used as LAN emulation, the pseudowire layer carries extra requirements. VPLS OAM relies on bidirectional Ethernet links or LAN segments, so failure in one direction or link fails the whole segment. When a partial mesh failure occurs in LAN emulation, either the entire pseudowire mesh should be shut down when only an entire VPLS is acceptable, or a subset of pseudowires should be shut down so that the remaining pseudowires have full connectivity among them when a partial VPLS is acceptable. Pseudowire OAM for the pseudowires related to a LAN emulation must allow detection of a partial mesh failure (R13a), allow the entire mesh to be shut down on detection of it (R13b), and allow a subset to be shut down so that a full mesh is present across the remaining subset (R13c). Shutting down in this way need not involve withdrawing labels.

Fault detection and recovery in LAN emulation relies on emulation recovery, so the fault detection and recovery time in the emulation should be less than the VPLS fault detection and recovery time, to prevent unnecessary switch-over and temporary flooding or looping within the customer OAM domain where a customer is dual-homed to the provider OAM domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The point-to-point service gets the same checklist, plus two extras that only make sense for a single circuit: detecting a circuit that is patched to the wrong place, and prioritizing the maintenance messages. Where the service is built as a mesh of emulated LANs, the requirements also say how to shut part of that mesh down when only one link breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The specification assumes that L2VPN components within the OAM domain are mutually trusted. On that assumption, confidentiality issues are fully addressed by filtering to prevent OAM frames from leaking outside their designated OAM domain. Authentication issues are addressed by preventing OAM frames generated outside a given OAM domain from entering the domain in question, and the requirements to prevent OAM messages from leaking outside a domain and for domains to be transparent to frames from higher-level domains are specified in the security sections for VPLS and VPWS. For additional levels of security, solutions may be required to encrypt and/or authenticate OAM frames inside an OAM domain, but those solutions are out of the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo trusts everything inside a maintenance area and treats the filtering at the boundary as the protection: frames do not leak out, and frames from outside are kept out unless they belong to a higher level. Encrypting the frames inside the area is mentioned as an option for operators who want more, and is not covered here.

viz.caption: HOW THE MAINTENANCE ENTITIES FIT TOGETHER

root.label: Maintenance Entity Group
root.note: The set of maintenance entities for one service instance.

children.label: Maintenance Entity
children.note: A point-to-point association between a pair of end points.

children.label: Maintenance End Point
children.note: Starts and stops OAM frames, at the edge of its OAM domain.

children.label: Maintenance Intermediate Point
children.note: Passes OAM frames but never initiates them.

viz.caption: EVERY LAYER OF THE SERVICE LOOKS AFTER ITSELF

layers.label: Service layer
layers.detail: VPLS, VPWS and IP-only LAN Service. Each is responsible for its own OAM.

layers.label: Network layer
layers.detail: MPLS and IP networks, whose own OAM covers the links between provider edges.

layers.label: Link technologies
layers.detail: SONET, Ethernet, ATM and others, each with its own capabilities.

viz.caption: THE VPLS REQUIREMENTS, IN THE ORDER THEY APPEAR

items.label: Discovery
items.desc: Find the other devices that share the same VPLS instance in the domain.

items.label: Fault detection
items.desc: Proactive connectivity monitoring between two VPLS-aware devices.

items.label: Fault verification
items.desc: Confirm that a detected fault is real.

items.label: Fault localization
items.desc: Pin the fault down to a device or a link.

items.label: Alarm suppression
items.desc: A transport fault triggers service-level notification so that redundant alarms are suppressed.

items.label: Frame loss
items.desc: Measure per-service frame or packet loss.

items.label: Two-way delay
items.desc: Measure round-trip delay, which needs no clock synchronisation.

items.label: One-way delay
items.desc: Measure one-way delay, which needs clock synchronisation.

items.label: Delay variation
items.desc: Measure per-service frame or packet delay variation.

items.label: Same path
items.desc: OAM frames must travel the same links and nodes as the service frames.

items.label: Scalability
items.desc: Support OAM for every VPLS instance the device supports.

items.label: Extensibility
items.desc: Allow new functions later, and let devices without OAM forward the frames.

items.label: Domain isolation
items.desc: Keep frames inside their own domain and pass higher-level frames transparently.

items.label: Transport independence
items.desc: Work the same whatever the underlying transport is.

items.label: Application independence
items.desc: Do not assume IP or any application-level OAM.
